instruction: none: started by the service for timer
headline: This run continued building the resting-contact method on branch method/rest, starting with spheres resting on the plate. That part now runs inside the simulation: a slow sphere is captured by the plate, rides it and is released, with its energy and momentum books closing to round-off, and with the method switched off the engine still passes the frozen engine tests. A real two-dimensional layer still stalls in its first cycle, where a sphere rests on top of a riding sphere. That case needs the moving stacks, which are not wired in yet.

questions.question: The next piece moves a sphere resting on a riding sphere together with it. Their smooth motion is integrated between exact events (adaptive steps at round-off accuracy, contact forces from a small linear solve, nothing corrected at steps). Is that within the plan, or does it count as time-stepping for you? (Asked last run; still unanswered.)
questions.why_it_matters: Tonight's layer showed that the method cannot run without this piece. The first stall is a sphere resting on a riding sphere. If you count it as time-stepping, sphere-on-sphere rest needs another approach.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Build it as designed (D0076) and report the share of sphere-time spent in integrated stacks once a layer runs, so it can be judged on numbers.

proposed_directions.direction: Wire moving stacks into the event loop next: a sphere hitting a riding sphere below the rest speed joins it in a stack, and the stack's contacts with free spheres are events. Fix the stack integrator's weakness the checker found (a push that dips below zero and recovers within one step) first.
proposed_directions.rationale: It is what stops the first layer. Every dense layer will have spheres resting on riding spheres within the first cycle.

proposed_directions.direction: Replay tonight's stall (scripts/rest_plate/stall.py on method/rest) as the first test of the stack build, then the 2D grid conditions.
proposed_directions.rationale: It is a small, exactly reproducible case where the plate part alone fails, so it shows at once whether stacks remove the chatter.

proposed_directions.direction: Once stacks run, measure the share of sphere-time spent in integrated stacks at the deep Gamma 5 conditions.
proposed_directions.rationale: It decides whether stacks are a cheap exception or a hidden time-stepper, the question put to Chris.

run_conditions.limits_hit: none. Only short local checks, each single-threaded: frozen tests twice (40 s each), method tests three times (about 25 s each), a 2D layer that stalled (143 s), event-by-event debugging and the stall trace (a few minutes). The CPU figure is the sum of those wall times, not read from ps. This ran on a Linux worker (40 cores, load 5.2 at start), not Chris's Mac, so pmset and memory_pressure are not available; budgets.yaml's local limits were checked against this machine's disk only. The data folder is 683 MB, including other lines' data. A stale numba cache cost one misleading failure: after a change to granular/rest_kernel.py, compiled engine functions kept the old version until the cache files were deleted. No experiments were registered: the checks above are development checks of the build (as in the previous run), described in evidence/L0009-build-2026-11-25-2.json and in PROGRAM.md.
